snippet.title: Why WWII Soldiers Sawed Off Their Shotguns?
snippet.description:
WWII shotgun tactics, close-quarters combat, sawed-off weapons — the surprising reason American troops shortened their shotguns.
How wide-spread shrapnel helped soldiers survive foxhole combat in World War II.

During World War II, some American soldiers deliberately sawed off the barrels of their shotguns.
The shortened barrel created a wider spread pattern, allowing pellets to cover more area with a single blast.
In tight foxholes and brutal close-quarters battles, this gave soldiers a life-saving advantage—
one shot could scatter multiple enemies long enough to escape or secure the position.
#militaryhistory #worldwar2

snippet.title: Advice for time traveling to medieval Europe
snippet.description:
Watch this video before visiting the European Middle Ages.

SUGGESTED READING

• Steven A. Epstein, An Economic and Social History of Later Medieval Europe, 1000–1500 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009).
• Urban Tignor Holmes, Jr., Daily Living in the Twelfth Century (Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 1952).
• Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (London: The Bodley Head, 2008).
• Paul B. Newman, Daily Life in the Middle Ages (Jefferson, N.C.: McFarland & Company, 2001).
• Jeffrey L. Singman, Daily Life in Medieval Europe (Westport, Conn.: Greenwood Press, 1999).


FAQ

• What about traveling there as a woman?
My advice applies to both men and women (except for the bit about clergy, obviously). Men and women will have to give the same amount of attention to constructing their backstory, including their marital status, because people will ask either way. Women went on pilgrimages. While most women (and men) worked on farms, women in towns did engage in economic activities like shopkeeping and weaving. It was rare for a woman to work as a long-distance merchant, but it did happen, typically as a widow whose husband had been a merchant.

• But what about a woman traveling alone?
When I said, "Travel in a group, don't travel alone," I meant it. Solo travel is not advised, regardless of gender. Even the medieval people themselves traveled in groups.


CORRECTIONS

• I said William of Rubruck was from the Netherlands but he was actually Flemish. Apologies to my Flemish viewers.
• In the anecdote where William of Rubruck met the Buddhist monks, he was confused at first but he did figure out in the course of talking to them that they were not Christian. I misremembered the passage. So I'd say Buddhists would probably just be understood as pagans in medieval Europe.
• The magic I discuss in the video is known as natural magic. There was also another form of magic I didn't talk about where you perform occult rituals to persuade demons to do things for you. That's known as demonic magic.

snippet.title: This Artist Carves Smiles Into Stone #HirotoshiIto #StoneArt #JapaneseArt #bizarre
snippet.description:
Japanese artist Hirotoshi Ito carves smiling faces into cold, hard stones - but his art reveals something deeper about human nature.

Ito finds river stones near his home in Japan and transforms them into his famous "Laughing Stones" by finding their cracks and breaking them open. His family has worked with stone since 1879, but his approach is unique.

"A smile on the beholder's face is the main motivation for my work," he says. Through his sculptures, Ito shows us that the coldest, hardest people often have the most warmth inside - they just hide it better.

His stone art serves as a powerful metaphor: sometimes the people who seem coldest simply need someone who sees past their protective exterior.

• Poor sanitation accelerated the spread of the plague

The real Viking winter story is far smarter and far more practical than the version most of us learned in school.

snippet.title: Why did Medieval Peasants Keep Stones Under Their Beds?
snippet.description:
Medieval heating tricks, Middle Ages survival, peasant life facts — the surprising reason peasants kept warm stones under their beds.How fire-heated stones protected families from freezing nights, drafts, and hypothermia.In the Middle Ages, most peasant homes were cold, drafty wooden huts with no insulation at all.Winters were brutal, and temperatures inside the house could drop low enough to threaten a person’s life during sleep.To survive the cold, peasants heated smooth stones in the fire, wrapped them in cloth, and placed them under their beds or blankets.
These simple “medieval heating stones” stayed warm for hours and were often the only source of nighttime heat for poor families.

snippet.description:
Why did some WWII soldiers go mad in the trenches?
Days of nonstop artillery fire shattered their nerves until their minds simply broke.
Many soldiers went more than 60 hours without sleep, hearing explosions even when the battlefield was silent.
Mud, disease, rats, and the constant smell of death pushed their sanity to its limit.
And when close friends died beside them, the trauma was often overwhelming.
For countless men, “madness” wasn’t weakness—
it was the human brain collapsing under the brutality of war.

snippet.title: Why Did Soldiers Use Soap to Seal Wounds in World War II?
snippet.description:
Why did some WWII soldiers use soap to seal wounds?
On the battlefield, medics often had no proper bandages and no time to treat every injury.
In emergencies, soldiers rubbed a bar of soap directly onto a bleeding cut.
The hardened soap created a temporary seal, slowing the blood until real medical help could arrive.
It wasn’t clean, safe, or ideal—
but in the chaos of war, a simple bar of soap could be the difference between life and death.

#SoldierLife #WW2

It wasn’t clean, safe, or ideal—
